questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The sum of the even multiples of 9 between 300 and 500 is
questions.solution:
Even multiples of 9 are of the form $18 n$.
$18 n$ for $n=1, \ldots, 27$ lies between 1 to 500
and $18 n$ for $n=1, \ldots, 16$ lies between 1 to 300 .
$\begin{aligned} \therefore \text{ Required sum } & =18\left[\sum_{n=1}^{27} n-\sum_{n=1}^{16} n\right] \\ & =18\left[\frac{27 \times 28}{2}-\frac{16 \times 17}{2}\right]=4356\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If geometric mean and harmonic mean of two numbers $a$ and $b$ are 16 and 64/5 respectively, then the value of $a: b$ is
questions.solution:
Geometric mean of $a$ and $b=\sqrt{a b}\Rightarrow \quad \sqrt{a b}=16$
(given)
$\Rightarrow \quad a b=256$....(i)
And harmonic mean of $a$ and $b=\frac{2 a b}{a+b}\therefore \quad \frac{2 a b}{a+b}=\frac{64}{5}$ (given)
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{2 \times 256}{a+b}=\frac{64}{5} \quad$ [from Eq. (i)]
$\therefore \quad \frac{2 a b}{a+b}=\frac{64}{5}$ (given)
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{2 \times 256}{a+b}=\frac{64}{5} \quad$ [from Eq. (i)]
$\Rightarrow \quad a+b=40$....(ii)
Now, $\quad(a-b)=\sqrt{(a+b)^2-4 a b}=\sqrt{(40)^2-4 \times 256}=\sqrt{1600-1024}=\sqrt{576}\Rightarrow \quad a-b=24$....(iii)
On solving Eqs. (ii) and (iii), we get
$a=32$ and $b=8\therefore \quad a: b=32: 8=4: 1$

questions.q: If expression $x+\frac{1}{x^2},|x\gt0|$ attains is minimum value at $x=\alpha$, then $\alpha^3$ is
questions.solution:
$\because  x+\frac{1}{x^2}=\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{x^2}\text{and } \mathrm{AM} \geq \mathrm{GM} \Rightarrow  \frac{x}{2}+\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{x^2} \geq\left(\frac{x}{2} \times \frac{x}{2} \times \frac{1}{x^2}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} \Rightarrow  \frac{x}{2}+\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{x^2} \geq\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}$
Minimum value of $x+\frac{1}{x^2}=\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{4}}$
and for minimum value
$\frac{x}{2}=\frac{1}{x^2} \Rightarrow x^3=2$
Hence, $\alpha^3=2$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \log _3 2, \log _3\left(2^x-5\right), \log _3\left(2^x-\frac{7}{2}\right) \text{ are$ in $AP. } \\ & \Rightarrow \log _3\left(2^x-5\right)=\frac{\log _3\left(2^x-\frac{7}{2}\right)+\log _3 2}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad\left(2^x-5\right)^2=2 \cdot\left(2^x-\frac{7}{2}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad\left(2^x\right)^2+25-10 \cdot 2^x=2 \cdot 2^x-7 \\ & \Rightarrow\left(2^x\right)^2-12 \cdot 2^x+25+7=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad\left(2^x\right)^2-12 \cdot 2^x+32=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 2^x=8 \text{ or } 2^x=4 \\ & \Rightarrow x=3 \text{ or } 2\end{aligned} \Rightarrow x=3(\because x=2$ does not satisfy the given series $)$

questions.q: If $a^2, b^2$ and $c^2$ are in AP, then $b+c, c+a$ and $a+b$ are in $\qquad$
questions.solution:
We have, $a^2, b^2$ and $c^2$ are in AP adding $a b+b c+c a$ to each of these terms, we get $a^2+a b+b c+c a, b^2+a b+b c+c a$ and $c^2+a b+b c+c a$ are in AP.
$\Rightarrow(a+b)(a+c),(b+c)(b+a) \text{ and }(c+a)(c+b)$ are in AP.
Dividing each term by $(b+c)(c+a)(a+b)$, we get
$\frac{1}{b+c}, \frac{1}{c+a}$ and $\frac{1}{a+b}$ are in AP
$\Rightarrow b+c, c+a$ and $a+b$ are in HP.

questions.q: If $a, b$ and $c$ are in HP, then for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$, which one of the following is true?
questions.solution:
Given that, $a, b$ and $c$ are in HP.
$\therefore$ Harmonic mean of $a$ and $c$ is $b$. and geometric mean of $a$ and $c$ is $\sqrt{a c}.
\because$ Geometric mean > Harmonic mean
$\Rightarrow \quad \sqrt{a c} > b$....(i)
Now, for the positive numbers $a^n$ and $c^n$, we have
Geometric mean $=\sqrt{a^n \cdot c^n}$
and arithmetic mean $=\frac{a^n+c^n}{2}\mathrm{AM} > \mathrm{GM}\begin{array}{ll}\therefore & \frac{a^n+c^n}{2} > \sqrt{a^n \cdot c^n} \\ \Rightarrow & a^n+c^n > 2 \sqrt{a^n \cdot c^n} \\ \Rightarrow & a^n+c^n > 2(\sqrt{a c})^n > 2 b^n \quad \text{ [using Eq. (i)] } \\ \Rightarrow & a^n+c^n > 2 b^n\end{array}$

questions.q: If $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ are in AP and $\tan ^{-1} \alpha, \tan ^{-1} \beta$ and $\tan ^{-1} \gamma$ are also in AP, then

\Rightarrow & \frac{\alpha+\gamma}{1-\beta^2} & =\frac{\alpha+\gamma}{1-\alpha \gamma} \quad \text{ ｂy using } \\

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Sum of the series to $n$ terms $5+7+13+31+85+\ldots$ is
questions.solution:
The sequence of differences between successive terms is $2,6,18,54, \ldots$.
Clearly, it is a GP. Let $T_n$ be the $n^{\text{th }}$ term of the given series and $S_n$ be the sum of its $n$ terms.
Then,
$S_n=5+7+13+31+85+\ldots+T_{n-1}+T_n$  ....(i)
$S_n=5+7+13+31+\ldots+I_{n-1}+I_n$  ...(ii)
Subtracting (ii) from (i), we get
$\begin{aligned} & \quad O=5+\left[2+6+18+54+\ldots+\left(T_n-T_{n-1}\right)\right]-T_n \\ & \Rightarrow \quad O=5+2 \cdot \frac{3^{n-1}-1}{3-1}-T_n \\ & \Rightarrow \quad T_n=5+\left(3^{n-1}-1\right)=4+3^{n-1} \\ & \begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n T_k=\sum_{k=1}^n\left(4+3^{k-1}\right) \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^n 4+\sum_{k=1}^n 3^{k-1} \\ & \quad=4 n+\left(1+3+3^2+\ldots+3^{n-1}\right)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =4 n+1 \times\left(\frac{5-1}{3-1}\right) \\ & =4 n+\left(\frac{3^n-1}{2}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left(3^n+8 n-1\right)\end{aligned}$

questions.q: In a triangle, the length of the two larger sides are 24 and 22 , respectively. If the angles are in AP , then the third side is
questions.solution:
Since the angles are in $A P$, therefore
$2 B=A+C \quad \Rightarrow \quad 3 B=A+B+C\Rightarrow 3 B=180^{{}^{\circ}} \Rightarrow B=60^{{}^{\circ}}$
using the formula,
$\frac{\sin A}{a}=\frac{\sin B}{b}$, we get
$\sin A=\frac{a}{b} \sin B=\frac{24}{22} \cdot \sin 60^{{}^{\circ}}=\frac{6 \sqrt{3}}{11}$
Now; $\quad \sin C=\sin \left(180^{{}^{\circ}}-(A+B)\right)=\sin (A+B)=\left(\frac{6 \sqrt{3}}{11}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\sqrt{\left\{1-\left(\frac{6 \sqrt{3}}{11}\right)^2\right\}} \cdot\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{22}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)(12+2 \sqrt{3})$
Now, $c=\frac{b}{\sin B} \sin C\Rightarrow \quad c=12+2 \sqrt{3}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
The sum to $n$ terms of the series:
$\frac{1}{1+1^2+1^4}+\frac{2}{1+2^2+2^4}+\frac{3}{1+3^2+3^4}+\ldots$ is
questions.solution:
Let $T_f$ be the $r^{\text {th }}$ term of the given series.
Then, $\quad T_r=\frac{r}{1+r^2+r^4}, \quad r=1,2,3, \ldots, n$
$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{r}{\left(r^2+r+1\right)\left(r^2-r+1\right)} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{r^2-r+1}-\frac{1}{r^2+r+1}\right]\end{aligned}$
$\therefore$ Sum of the series $=\sum_{r=1}^n T_r$
$=\frac{1}{2}\left\{\sum_{r=1}^n\left(\frac{1}{r^2-r+1}-\frac{1}{r^2+r+1}\right)\right\}$
$\begin{array}{r}=\frac{1}{2}\left\{\left(1-\frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{7}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{7}-\frac{1}{13}\right)+\ldots+\right. \\ \left.\left(\frac{1}{n^2-n+1}-\frac{1}{n^2+n+1}\right)\right\}\end{array}$
$=\frac{1}{2}\left\{1-\frac{1}{n^2+n+1}\right\}=\frac{n^2+n}{2\left(n^2+n+1\right)}$

questions.q: The sum of the series $1+\frac{2^2}{2!}+\frac{3^2}{3!}+\frac{4^2}{4!}+\ldots$ is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \text{ Let } S=1+\frac{2^2}{2!}+\frac{3^2}{3!}+\frac{4^2}{4!}+\ldots \\

questions.q: $1+\frac{3}{1!}+\frac{5}{2!}+\frac{7}{3!}+\ldots \infty$ is

$\therefore \quad T_n=\frac{(2 n-1)}{(n-1)!} ; n=1,2,3, \ldots, \infty\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad T_n & =\frac{2 n}{(n-1)!}-\frac{1}{(n-1)!} \\ & =2\left[\frac{(n-1)}{(n-1)!}+\frac{1}{(n-1)!}\right]-\frac{1}{(n-1)!} \\ & =\frac{2}{(n-2)!}+\frac{1}{(n-1)!} \\ \therefore \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} T_n & =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2}{(n-2)!}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(n-1)!} \\ & =2 e+e=3 e\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the sum of four numbers in GP is 60 and the arithmetic mean of the first and last numbers is 18 then the numbers are
questions.solution:
Let four terms in a GP be $a r^3, a r, \frac{a}{r}$ and $\frac{a}{r^3}$.
According to the given condition,
$a r^3+a r+\frac{a}{r}+\frac{a}{r^3}=60$  ....(i)
and $\quad \frac{a r^3+\frac{a}{r^3}}{2}=18\Rightarrow \quad a r^3+\frac{a}{r^3}=36$  .....(ii)
Now, from Eq. (i), we have
$\left(a r+\frac{a}{r}\right)+a r^3+\frac{a}{r^3}=60\Rightarrow \quad a\left(r+\frac{1}{r}\right)+36=60 \quad$ [from Eq. (ii)]
$\Rightarrow \quad a\left(r+\frac{1}{r}\right)=24$  .....(iii)
On dividing Eq. (iii) by Eq. (ii), we get
$\frac{a\left(r^3+\frac{1}{r^3}\right)}{a\left(r+\frac{1}{r}\right)}=\frac{36}{24}\Rightarrow \frac{\left(r+\frac{1}{r}\right)\left(r^2+\frac{1}{r^2}-1\right)}{r+\frac{1}{r}}=\frac{3}{2}\Rightarrow \quad 2\left(r^2+\frac{1}{r^2}-1\right)=3\Rightarrow \quad \frac{2\left(r^4+1-r^2\right)}{r^2}=3$\begin{array}{lc}\Rightarrow & 2 r^4+2-2 r^2=3 r^2 \\ \Rightarrow & 2 r^4-5 r^2+2=0 \\ \Rightarrow & 2 r^4-4 r^2-r^2+2=0 \\ \Rightarrow & 2 r^2 $\left(r^2-2\right)$-1 $\left(r^2-2\right)$=0 \\ \Rightarrow & $\left(r^2-2\right) \left(2 r^2-1\right)=0 \\ \Rightarrow & r^2=2,2 r^2=1 \\ \Rightarrow & r= \pm \sqrt{2}, r= \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{array}$
On putting $r=\sqrt{2}$ in Eq. (iii), we get
$a\left(\sqrt{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=24\Rightarrow \quad a \left(\frac{2+1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=24\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & 3 a & =24 \sqrt{2} \\ \Rightarrow & a & =8 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}\therefore$ Series becomes $8 \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2})^3, 8 \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}), \frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^3}$ i.e., $32,16,8$ and 4.
If we take $r=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, we get the series
4, 8, 16 and 32.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $x>1, y>1, z>1$ are in GP, then $\frac{1}{1+\ln x}\frac{1}{1+\ln y}, \frac{1}{1+\ln z}$ are in
questions.solution:
Let the common ratio of the GP be $r$. Then, $y=x r and z=x r^2$.
$\Rightarrow \quad \ln y=\ln x+\ln r$ and $\ln z=\ln x+2 \ln r$
Putting $A=1+\ln x, D=\ln r$
Then, $\quad \frac{1}{1+\ln x}=\frac{1}{A}$,
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{1+\ln y}=\frac{1}{1+\ln x r}=\frac{1}{1+\ln x+\ln r}=\frac{1}{A+D} \\
& \text{$ and $} \frac{1}{1+\ln z}=\frac{1}{1+\ln x+2 \ln r}=\frac{1}{A+2 D}
\end{aligned}$
Here we see that $A, A+D and A+2 D$ are in AP. $\therefore \frac{1}{A}, \frac{1}{A+D}$ and $\frac{1}{A+2 D}$ are in HP.
Therefore, $\frac{1}{1+\ln x}, \frac{1}{1+\ln y}, \frac{1}{1+\ln z}$, are in HP.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\frac{e^x}{1-x}=B_0+B_1 x+B_2 x^2+\ldots+B_n x^n+\ldots$ then $B_n-B_{n-1}$ equals
questions.solution:
We have,
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{e^x}{1-x}=B_0+B_1 x+B_2 x^2+\ldots+B_n x^n+\ldots \\
& \Rightarrow e^x(1-x)^{-1}=B_0+B_1 x+B_2 x^2+\ldots+B_n x^n+\ldots \\
& \Rightarrow\left(1+\frac{x}{1!}+\frac{x^2}{2!}+\ldots+\frac{x^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}+\frac{x^n}{n!}+\ldots\right) \times \\
& \quad\left(1+x+x^2+\ldots+x^{n-1}+x^n+\ldots \infty\right) \\
& \quad=B_0+B_1 x+B_2 x^2+\ldots+B_n x^n+\ldots
\end{aligned}$On comparing the coefficients of $x^n and x^{n-1}$ on both sides, we get
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{n!}+\frac{1}{(n-1)!}+\ldots+\frac{1}{2!}+\frac{1}{1!}+1=B_n \\ & \begin{aligned} & \text{$ and $} \frac{1}{(n-1)!}+\frac{1}{(n-2)!}+\ldots+\frac{1}{2!}+\frac{1}{1!}+1 \\ &=B_{n-1} \\ & B_n-B_{n-1}=\frac{1}{n!}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The harmonic mean of the root of the equation $(5+\sqrt{2}) x^2-(4+\sqrt{5}) x+8+2 \sqrt{5}=0$ is
questions.solution:
Let $\alpha, \beta$ be the roots of given quadratic equation. Then,
$\alpha+\beta=\frac{4+\sqrt{5}}{5+\sqrt{2}} \text{ and } \alpha \beta=\frac{8+2 \sqrt{5}}{5+\sqrt{2}}$
Again, $H$ be the harmonic mean between $\alpha$ and $\beta$, then $H=\frac{2 \alpha \beta}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac{16+4 \sqrt{5}}{4+\sqrt{5}}=4$

questions.q: If $\alpha \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right),$ then $\sqrt{x^2+x}+\frac{\tan ^2 \alpha}{\sqrt{x^2+x}}$ is always greater than or equal to
questions.solution:
Here, $\alpha \in\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \Rightarrow \tan \alpha$ is (+ve)
As, we know, if $a, b>0 \Rightarrow \frac{a+b}{2} \geq \sqrt{a b}$
i.e., $\quad \mathrm{AM} \geq \mathrm{GM}\begin{aligned}
\therefore & \frac{\sqrt{x^2+x}+\frac{\tan ^2 \alpha}{\sqrt{x^2+x}}}{2} \geq \sqrt{\sqrt{x^2+x} \cdot \frac{\tan ^2 \alpha}{\sqrt{x^2+x}}} \\
& \qquad(\text{ using } \mathrm{AM} \geq \mathrm{GM})
\end{aligned}\Rightarrow \quad \sqrt{x^2+x}+\frac{\tan ^2 \alpha}{\sqrt{x^2+x}} \geq 2 \tan \alpha$

questions.q: Suppose $a, b, c$ are in AP and $a^2, b^2, c^2$ are in GP. If $a < b < c$ and $a+b+c=\frac{3}{2}$, then the value of $a$ is
questions.solution:
Since, $a, b, c$ are in AP.
$\therefore \quad a=A-D, b=A, c=A+D$
Where, $A$ is the first term and $D$ is the common difference of an AP.
Given,
$a+b+c=\frac{3}{2}$
$\begin{array}{rrr}
\Rightarrow & (A-D)+A+(A+D) & =\frac{3}{2} \\
\Rightarrow & 3 A & =\frac{3}{2} \\
\Rightarrow & A & =\frac{1}{2}
\end{array}$
$\therefore$ The numbers are $\frac{1}{2}-D, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}+D$
Also, $\left(\frac{1}{2}-D\right)^2, \frac{1}{4},\left(\frac{1}{2}+D\right)^2$ are in GP.
$\Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2=\left(\frac{1}{2}-D\right)^2\left(\frac{1}{2}+D\right)^2$
$\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & \frac{1}{16}=\left(\frac{1}{4}-D^2\right)^2 \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{1}{4}-D^2= \pm \frac{1}{4} \\
\Rightarrow & \quad D^2=\left(\frac{1}{2} D=0 \text{ is not possible }\right) \\
\Rightarrow & D= \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
\therefore & a=\frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{array}$
So, out of the given value $a=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ is the right choice.

questions.q: If the roots of the cubic equation $a x^3+b x^2+c x+d=0$ are in GP, then
questions.solution:
Let $\frac{A}{R}, A, A R$ be the roots of the equation $a x^3+b x^2+c x+d=0$, then Product of roots
$\begin{aligned} & A^3=-\frac{d}{a} \\ \Rightarrow \quad= & A=-\left(\frac{d}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}\end{aligned}$
Since, $A$ is a root of the equation.
$\therefore \quad a A^3+b A^2+c A+d=0\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad a\left(-\frac{d}{a}\right)+b\left(-\frac{d}{a}\right)^{2 / 3}+c\left(-\frac{d}{a}\right)^{1 / 3}+d=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad b\left(\frac{d}{a}\right)^{2 / 3}=c\left(\frac{d}{a}\right)^{1 / 3} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad b^3 \cdot \frac{d^2}{a^2}=c^3 \cdot \frac{d}{a} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad b^3 d=c^3 a\end{aligned}$

questions.q: $The sum of the series \frac{3}{4 \cdot 8}-\frac{3 \cdot 5}{4 \cdot 8 \cdot 12}+\frac{3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7}{4 \cdot 8 \cdot 12 \cdot 16}-\ldots$ is
questions.solution: $\frac{3}{4 \cdot 8}-\frac{3 \cdot 5}{4 \cdot 8 \cdot 12}+\frac{3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7}{4 \cdot 8 \cdot 12 \cdot 16}-\ldots+\frac{3}{4}-\frac{3}{4}\begin{aligned} & =1-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1 \cdot 3}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 4}-\frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5}{4 \cdot 4 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 3}+\ldots-\frac{3}{4} \\ & =\left[1+\frac{1}{1!}\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)+\frac{1(1+2)}{2!}\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)^2\right.+\frac{1(1+2)(1+4)}{3!}\left(-\frac{1}{4}^3+\ldots\right]-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}=\left(1-\frac{1}{4}\right)^{-1 / 2}-\frac{3}{4}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}-\frac{3}{4}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The sum to $n$ terms of the series $\frac{3}{1^2}+\frac{5}{1^2+2^2}+\frac{7}{1^2+2^2+3^2}+\ldots$, is
questions.solution:
Let $T_r$ be the $r$ th term of the given series. Then,
$T_r=\frac{2 r+1}{1^2+2^2+\ldots+r^2}=\frac{2 r+1}{\frac{r(r+1)(2 r+1)}{6}}=\frac{6}{r(r+1)}\Rightarrow \quad T_r=6 \left(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{r+1}\right)
So, the required sum is given by
$\sum_{r=1}^n T_r=6 \sum_{r=1}^n$\left(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{r+1}\right)\begin{aligned}$& =6$\left[\frac{1}{1}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}+\ldots+\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right]$\\ & =6\l$left[1-\frac{1}{n+1}\right]=\frac{6 n}{n+1}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The sum to infinity of the series $1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{6}{3^2}+\frac{10}{3^3}+\frac{14}{3^4}+\ldots$ is
questions.solution:
Let $S$ be the sum of the given series.
i.e.
$S=1+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{6}{3^2}+\frac{10}{3^3}+\ldots\Rightarrow \quad(S-1)=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{6}{3^2}+\frac{10}{3^3}+\ldots$ ...(i)
$\Rightarrow \quad(S-1) \times \frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3^2}+\frac{6}{3^3}+\frac{10}{3^4}+\ldots$ ...(ii)
On subtracting Eq. (ii) from Eq. (i), we get
$\frac{2}{3}(S-1)=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{4}{3^2}+\frac{4}{3^3}+\frac{4}{3^4}+\ldots\Rightarrow \frac{2}{3}(S-1)=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\frac{4}{3^2}}{1-\frac{1}{3}}\Rightarrow \frac{2}{3}(S-1)=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\Rightarrow S-1 \Rightarrow S=3$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The sum of $n$ terms of the series $+1+\frac{4}{5}+\frac{7}{5^2}+\frac{10}{5^3}+\ldots$ is
questions.solution:
Clearly, the given series is an arithmetico-geometric series whose corresponding AP and GP. are respectively, $1,4,7,10, \ldots$ and $1, \frac{1}{5}, \frac{1}{5^2}, \frac{1}{5^3}, \ldots$
The $n^{\text{th }}$ term of $A P=[1+(n-1) \times 3]=3 n-2$
The $n^{\text{th }}$ term of GP $=\left[1 \times\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{n-1}\right]=\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{n-1}$
So, the $n^{\text{th }}$ term of the given series is
$(3 n-2) \times \frac{1}{5^{n-1}}=\frac{3 n-2}{5^{n-1}}$
Let, $\quad \begin{aligned} S_n=1+\frac{4}{5}+\frac{7}{5^2} & +\frac{10}{5^3}+\ldots \\ & +\frac{3 n-5}{5^{n-2}}+\frac{3 n-2}{5^{n-1}}\end{aligned}$ ...(i)
$\frac{1}{5} S_n=\frac{1}{5}+\frac{4}{5^2}+\frac{7}{5^3}+\ldots+\frac{(3 n-5)}{5^{n-1}}+\frac{3 n-2}{5^n}$ ....(ii)
Subtracting (ii) from (i), we get
$\begin{aligned} S_n-\frac{1}{5} S_n=1+\left\{\frac{3}{5}+\frac{3}{5^2}+\frac{3}{5^3}+\ldots+\frac{3}{5^{n-1}}\right\} \\ -\frac{(3 n-2)}{5^n}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{4}{5} S_n=1+\frac{3}{5} \frac{\left\{1-\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{n-1}\right\}}{\left(1-\frac{1}{5}\right)}-\frac{(3 n-2)}{5^n} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{4}{5} S_n=1+\frac{3}{5} \frac{\left\{1-\frac{1}{5^{n-1}}\right\}}{\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)}-\frac{(3 n-2)}{5^n} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{4}{5} S_n=1+\frac{3}{4}\left(1-\frac{1}{5^{n-1}}\right)-\frac{(3 n-2)}{5^n} \\ & \Rightarrow S_n=\frac{5}{4}+\frac{15}{16}\left(1-\frac{1}{5^{n-1}}\right)-\frac{(3 n-2)}{4 \cdot 5^{n-1}}\end{aligned}$
